item.title: OpenAI audit finds about 30% of SWE-Bench Pro coding tasks are flawed, raising concerns about AI model evaluation accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI conducted a detailed audit of SWE-Bench Pro, a widely used coding benchmark, and found that approximately 30% of its tasks are broken due to issues like overly strict tests, underspecified prompts, low test coverage, and misleading instructions. These flaws undermine the benchmark's reliability in measuring AI coding capabilities and could misrepresent model performance and safety assessments. The audit involved an automated data quality pipeline, agent-assisted reviews, and a human annotation campaign with experienced software engineers. The findings highlight the challenges in creating fair and effective benchmarks for AI coding models and suggest that developers should carefully scrutinize evaluation results when using SWE-Bench Pro.

item.title: SpaceXAI launches Grok 4.5, its most advanced model for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work with improved efficiency and real-world engineering performance [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SpaceXAI has introduced Grok 4.5, its smartest AI model designed to excel in coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work. Trained on extensive datasets covering coding, science, engineering, and math, Grok 4.5 delivers intelligent and efficient reasoning, outperforming comparable leading models in real engineering tasks. The model was developed using tens of thousands of NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with advanced data curation and reinforcement learning techniques focused on multi-step software engineering tasks. Grok 4.5 operates at fast speeds with twice the token efficiency of leading models, reducing costs and processing time. It is now the default model in Grok Build, capable of creating complex Excel models, PowerPoint diagrams, and Word documents with minimal prompts. The model is priced competitively at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens and is available via the SpaceXAI API and products, with EU availability expected in mid-July.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-Live, a new full-duplex voice model for natural, continuous human-AI conversation using GPT-5.5 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-Live, a next-generation voice model designed for more natural and fluid human-AI interaction by enabling simultaneous listening and speaking. GPT-Live can engage in back-and-forth conversation, use filler phrases to show attention, and delegate complex tasks to GPT-5.5 running in the background, maintaining conversational flow while performing deeper reasoning or web searches. GPT-Live improves on previous voice AI systems by using a full-duplex architecture that processes input and output continuously rather than in discrete turns, reducing interruptions and latency. OpenAI is rolling out two versions, GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1 mini, to ChatGPT users globally and plans to offer API access for developers and enterprises soon. Human evaluations show GPT-Live outperforms earlier voice modes in conversational naturalness, reasoning, and information retrieval.

item.title: Microsoft releases Flint, a visualization language designed for AI agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Microsoft has launched Flint, a new visualization language aimed at improving the way AI agents are represented and understood. The tool is intended to help developers and researchers create clearer visualizations of AI agent behaviors and interactions. Flint is available through Microsoft's GitHub pages and has sparked discussion among developers interested in AI visualization techniques. The release reflects ongoing efforts to enhance transparency and interpretability in AI systems.

item.title: Databricks benchmarks coding agents on multi-million line codebase, finding mixed model performance and cost efficiency across OpenAI, Anthropic, and open source tools [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Databricks conducted an internal benchmark of coding agents using real engineering tasks on its multi-million line codebase, covering languages like Python, Go, Typescript, and Scala. The study evaluated models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and open source projects, revealing distinct capability tiers and highlighting that a combination of models offers the best cost-performance balance for different coding tasks. The analysis showed that open models such as GLM 5.2 can handle complex tasks effectively and cost-efficiently, while token price alone is a poor predictor of total task cost due to differences in model efficiency. Additionally, the choice of harness significantly impacts both cost and quality, with simpler harnesses like Pi often outperforming others by managing context more efficiently. These insights have informed Databricks' strategy to optimize model use for various engineering workloads.

item.title: Analysis finds 97% of websites lack AI agent-accessible tools, limiting AI interaction despite strong technical readiness [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A recent study analyzed nearly 10,000 websites to assess their readiness for AI agents to interact and act on them, finding that 97% expose no tools or interfaces usable by AI agents. While most sites meet technical basics like HTTPS and mobile rendering, they fail to provide actionable APIs or endpoints, making the web largely unreadable for AI beyond simple content consumption. The study also revealed that AI can understand marketing content well but struggles to answer commercial questions such as pricing, refund policies, and sign-up processes, scoring an average of 43 out of 100 on cost-related queries. Websites tend to be either clearly legible to AI or almost entirely opaque, with few in between, indicating a significant divide in AI accessibility across the web.

item.title: Brown University professor suspects majority of his economics class used AI to cheat on take-home midterm, leading to in-person final exam and many failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Brown University economics professor Roberto Serrano suspects that most students in his large welfare economics class used artificial intelligence tools to complete a take-home midterm exam, resulting in unusually high scores. In response, he required an in-person final exam, which led to many students dropping the course or failing, and he ultimately voided the midterm results due to suspected cheating. Serrano noted that the midterm average was 96 percent, far above historical averages, and that AI-generated answers closely matched student submissions. After the in-person final exam yielded much lower scores, he concluded widespread AI-assisted cheating had occurred. The university's academic committee requested individual complaints against suspected students, but Serrano and supporters criticized the administration's response as insufficient and ineffective in addressing AI-enabled cheating at scale.

item.title: Compass reports over 140 San Francisco homes sold for $1M above asking price in H1 2026 amid AI-driven wealth surge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: San Francisco's housing market has seen unprecedented overbidding, with more than 140 homes selling for at least $1 million above asking price in the first half of 2026, driven by rapid AI industry growth. This surge contrasts sharply with just eight such sales in the same period last year, reflecting increased wealth and demand linked to AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic preparing for major IPOs. Compass's analysis highlights a 17% year-over-year rise in single-family home prices and a 45% drop in inventory, with homes selling in an average of 18 days, the fastest pace in five years. The demand is concentrated in luxury markets near AI employment centers, contributing to aggressive bidding wars and rising rents, marking a shift from previous years when concerns about crime and homelessness had dampened the market. The trend is unique to San Francisco among tech hubs, with the city now having the highest median home price in the U.S. Experts note that AI-driven prosperity is concentrated among a small segment of the population, intensifying housing market segmentation by income and location.

item.title: OpenAI's AI wins all five problems at AtCoder World Tour Finals 2026, outperforming all human competitors in a top programming contest [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: At the AtCoder World Tour Finals 2026 in Japan, an OpenAI AI system defeated all human finalists in an exhibition match by solving all five problems in the Algorithm Division, including two rated exceptionally difficult. The AI finished first with 8,300 points, nearly doubling the runner-up's score, and no human solved the two hardest problems. The AI's performance marked a significant improvement over previous years, with the system solving problems that stumped both humans and itself for hours before finally cracking them. The model, comparable to GPT-5.6 and running without internet access, demonstrated advanced reasoning capabilities, surpassing earlier AI achievements at similar competitions such as the International Olympiad in Informatics and the ICPC World Finals. OpenAI highlighted that the system was not specifically trained for this contest but used a general reasoning model ensemble. The company plans to target the International Olympiad in Informatics 2026 next, continuing its rapid progress in competitive programming AI.

item.title: Anthropic reiterates ban on Claude access in China amid Beijing's backdoor security warning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has reaffirmed its policy prohibiting access to its Claude AI models and coding tools in China following a recent warning from the Chinese government about a potential security backdoor in Claude Code. The U.S.-based company responded to Beijing's claims by denying the existence of any hidden backdoor as described in the warning.

item.title: Isnad launches Python framework applying 1,200-year-old Islamic trust system to improve AI multi-agent reliability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Isnad is an open-source Python framework inspired by the classical Islamic isnād system, designed to track and evaluate trustworthiness across chains of AI agents in multi-agent systems. It models each AI agent as a narrator with a reliability grade, propagating trust through the chain and using weakest-link evaluation to identify where errors may occur. The framework aims to address provenance challenges in AI pipelines by recording the sequence of agents contributing to a claim and adjusting confidence based on each agent's reliability. Isnad includes a public research paper, unit-tested code, and early experiments showing that grading agents can reduce error rates compared to ungated AI serving. It is model-agnostic and intended to integrate with tools like LangChain to improve AI trust and verification.

item.title: Google patches AI chatbot vulnerability that risked exposing customer conversations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google fixed a security flaw in its AI chatbot that could have allowed unauthorized access to customer conversations. The issue raised concerns about data privacy and the protection of sensitive information handled by AI systems. The patch aims to strengthen the chatbot's security measures and prevent similar vulnerabilities in the future.

item.title: UK plans to ban romantic AI chatbots for users under 18 as part of broader online safety measures [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The UK government announced plans to prohibit users under 18 from accessing AI chatbots designed for romantic or sexual roleplay, aligning with new restrictions on social media use for under-16s. This policy aims to address distinct online risks faced by young people, particularly regarding AI systems that simulate romantic companionship. Researchers involved in the SHIFT-AI project, working with young people aged 16 to 24, found that while romantic AI chatbots pose some risks, young people are more concerned about issues like over-reliance on AI for emotional support, misplaced trust in AI advice, and cognitive impacts from habitual AI use. The researchers also questioned the rationale behind setting the age limit at 18, noting inconsistencies with legal rights related to consent in the UK. Experts suggest that instead of bans, regulation should focus on fostering AI literacy and designing AI systems that support adolescent agency and critical engagement. They warn that age-based restrictions without clear evidence may undermine young people's competence and fail to address the broader risks they face with AI technologies.

item.title: burn2kicad launches tool to convert simple text netlists and component directories into KiCad projects for AI agent use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: burn2kicad is a new tool that converts a small component asset directory and a text netlist into a KiCad project, simplifying the design process for AI agents by avoiding the complexities of KiCad's file formats. Users create an input directory with component symbols, footprints, datasheets, and optional 3D models, then run burn2kicad to generate a schematic with labeled net stubs and project-local libraries. burn2kicad supports initialization of input directories, dry-run previews, and copies necessary files into the output project folder, enabling streamlined circuit design workflows for AI-driven automation and development.

item.title: Chat Privacy extension hides AI chat history sidebars during screen sharing to protect sensitive information on supported chat platforms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Chat Privacy is a browser extension designed to hide AI chat history sidebars on supported websites during screen sharing, recordings, and public use to prevent accidental exposure of private conversation details. It offers a simple toggle to show or hide chat histories, helping users maintain privacy and focus while working with AI chat tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others. The extension does not access or share chat content, uses no tracking or analytics, and controls only the local display of chat history lists. It is aimed at developers, consultants, educators, and remote workers who want to protect sensitive information such as client names, project details, and personal plans during screen sharing or public computer use.

item.title: Open-source Wallie AI streams, sees, hears, and plays Minecraft with grounded commentary and customizable personas [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Wallie is an open-source AI system that can visually perceive its environment, hear audio, react in real time, and play Minecraft autonomously while providing commentary based on its actual in-game state. It runs locally on users' machines, allowing full customization of its personality, voice, and behavior without relying on cloud services. Wallie supports long streaming sessions with memory retention and natural pacing, aiming to deliver a more lifelike AI streamer experience compared to existing demos. The system integrates with various large language models, text-to-speech engines, and chat platforms, and includes features like goal-driven gameplay, smooth camera control, and a dashboard for easy setup and configuration.

item.title: Agentic FC launches AI-driven football management simulation using MCP platform with autonomous managers and live spectator console [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Agentic FC is a football management simulation game where AI agents autonomously manage clubs through the MCP platform, making decisions on transfers, tactics, and player management while providing an auditable history. The game features a live terminal-based spectator console that displays matches, league tables, and commentary in real time. Developed in Go, Agentic FC supports seeded persistent worlds with deterministic simulation, allowing reproducible seasons and matches influenced by player attributes, injuries, and board interactions. The project is under active development with a public API and save format still evolving, and it emphasizes AI-first management where agents shape a manager's mindset rather than issuing individual commands.

item.title: Internationalizationstack launches CLI tools and translation skills to fix AI localization bugs in Claude Code across 46 languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Internationalizationstack is a new toolset designed to address localization bugs in Claude Code by providing a full localization workflow including format conversion, pseudo-translation, native-quality translation skills, and validation. It supports 46 languages with language-specific rules to improve AI handling of internationalization issues. The toolset installs via a single command and integrates with Claude Code, offering CLI tools and slash commands for converting source files, pseudo-translating to detect hardcoded strings, translating with native-writer rules, and validating translations before release. It aims to streamline shipping new locales end to end and can be updated or uninstalled through simple commands.

item.title: Report finds KPMG's 2025 AI-focused customer experience study contains mostly fabricated or inaccurate citations, raising concerns about AI hallucinations in consulting research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An investigation by GPTZero into KPMG's October 2025 report on customer experience and agentic AI revealed that out of 45 citations, only five accurately referenced real sources, while the majority were fabricated, paraphrased, or too vague to verify. The report, part of KPMG's Global Customer Experience Excellence study, appears to have used AI-powered tools that generated numerous hallucinated citations, a phenomenon where AI produces false or misleading references. This raises questions about the reliability of AI-generated research outputs in major consulting firms and highlights challenges in managing AI hallucinations in professional reports.

item.title: xAI releases Grok 4.5, a coding-focused AI model priced significantly lower than Fable 5 and GPT-5.5 despite trailing in some benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: xAI has launched Grok 4.5, an AI model trained on tens of thousands of Nvidia GB300 GPUs targeting coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work. While Grok 4.5 scores close to GPT-5.5 and Fable 5 on some benchmarks, it falls behind on others, particularly in resolving real GitHub issues and harder software engineering problems. The model is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, substantially cheaper than competitors like Fable 5 and GPT-5.5, which may offset its performance gaps for many users. Grok 4.5 uses data filtering and reinforcement learning focused on software engineering tasks, achieving efficiency by requiring 4.2 times fewer tokens than Opus 4.8 on certain benchmarks. It is available now through Grok Build, Cursor, and the xAI console, with plugins for Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel. The model is expected to launch in the EU by mid-July. xAI developed Grok 4.5 alongside the code editor Cursor, recently acquired by SpaceX.

Organizations need to carefully assess and mitigate these risks to ensure responsible and effective use of AI in marketing operations.

item.title: China Plans to Let Top AI Firms Buy Limited Amount of Nvidia H200 Chips [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: China plans to allow some of the country's biggest AI companies to buy a small number of Nvidia's H200 chips, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The chip purchase approvals would offset a shortage caused by soaring demand for AI chips. U.S. President Donald Trump gave Nvidia permission in December to ship H200 chips to approved Chinese customers-a major shift in Washington's export control policy, as the H200 had previously been off-limits to China. Beijing, however, had not yet given local companies permission to buy the chips, out of protection for domestic chipmakers.

item.title: AI Borrowers Tap a $3.5 Trillion Market Hiding in Plain Sight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The longer I cover the money behind AI, the more I learn about new markets opening up to data center developers or operators, chip manufacturers and others looking for money to build ambitious AI projects. That's what makes this job so interesting. For the past several months, I've been wondering about a market I keep hearing referred to by the Securities Act of 1933 rule that governs it: Rule 144A. One banker called the market "a new tool in the toolkit" for data center developers. So what's going on exactly? The simple answer, at least in securities law terms, is that Rule 144A provides a safe harbor for the resale of privately placed securities. It effectively creates a market with many of the perks of a public bond or equity sale. Unlike a traditional private placement, these securities can be traded between sophisticated investors even though they're not registered for public sale. Data center developers sell the securities to investment banks, who immediately resell them, under the shelter of the safe harbor, to institutional investors managing $100 million or more in assets. Smaller investors are off-limits, but the additional liquidity can help developers raise money on better terms while still avoiding the full public disclosure process. At least three publicly traded data center developers tapped it in June alone, some returning for their second or third helping of fresh financing for new data center projects. While the market is hardly a secret to Wall Street bankers, it remains mostly invisible to the public. One banker I talked to about these deals called it "the biggest market you've never heard about." Exact numbers are tough to come by. According to one estimate, the investment-grade portion of the 144A market is roughly $3.5 trillion in size. That's still less than half the $8 trillion in Securities and Exchange Commission-registered U.S. investment-grade bonds. Companies with non-investment-grade ratings on their debt also tap the 144A market, as do equity issuers. Some $448 billion of 144A debt has been sold this year, putting it on track to surpass last year's total of $615 billion, according to data provided by the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. Meta Platforms raised $27 billion last October by issuing 144A bonds through a joint venture it formed with Blue Owl, Beignet Investor LLC, to fund a data center development in Richland Parish, La. Bond giant Pimco bought about $18 billion of the bonds and parceled that out to its various funds and other partners. The deal made a splash, though most of the attention was on its size and joint venture structure rather than the market into which the bonds sold. Data center developers didn't miss the deal's significance, and with the help of their bankers, TeraWulf, Cipher Mining, Applied Digital and others soon followed suit, raising billions of dollars through 144A private placements. Late last month, Sharon AI, the Australia-based neocloud, used the market to sell convertible notes. Since May 2025, data center developers or neoclouds have issued $71.9 billion across 26 transactions in the 144A private placement market, according to Dealogic data. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs count among the busiest banks helping them. Clearly the market is big enough to swallow a large chunk of the massive capital needed for AI infrastructure. What's more intriguing is why companies like Meta, Blue Owl and TeraWulf, which already have access to public markets, are turning to private placements in the first place. Historically, if a company wanted to build a data center, it could get a construction loan from a bank or a collection of banks, or it could turn to project finance lenders. That model worked for established developers with a strong track record; the banks that make loans in those markets are willing to take construction risk, but they generally don't like to take chances on unproven developers. More recently, many smaller, AI-focused developers have created webs of subsidiaries below their parent companies to hold individual data center projects. Meta too has created special purpose vehicles. Those structures help isolate risk from the parent companies, but they also leave the project vehicles with no track record and potentially limit lenders' ability to seek repayment if things go south. A company like Meta could likely still arrange financing to build a data center, but it would be tougher for former bitcoin miners turned AI data center developers to do so, one of the bankers said. That's where the 144A market comes in, giving the entities a way to tap bond markets to finance big projects without issuing registered public debt. One banker described it as a "market of necessity," not choice. In such a structure, the 144A debt is backed by cash flows coming from the ultimate tenant of the finished data center, in many cases a large hyperscaler or leading AI lab. With that backing, institutional investors can get comfortable with buying the private placement debt. Tapping the capital markets in this way allows issuers to access more leverage, according to David de Boltz, a managing director in technology leveraged finance at JPMorgan. Some of the 144A private placements have allowed for borrowing of up to 90% to 95% of the project's cost, meaning developers only need to put up a relatively small amount in equity. That compares to project finance loans that more typically cap the leverage at 60 to 80 cents of every dollar in project cost. "What that means is you do not need to go and raise too much equity to finance these projects," he said. These bonds also let issuers move quickly, since many project finance loans take more time to negotiate, and it allows borrowers to provide just enough financial disclosure to get investors on board. In the case of an SPV or a subsidiary, investors might only get financial data on that entity and how it planned to repay its debt, rather than getting the broader picture of the parent company. The 144A route doesn't come without downsides. Private placements are excluded from bond indices such as the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index, which means index-tracking investors aren't required to buy them. Other investors may have mandates that don't let them buy private placements at all, further limiting potential buyers. The market seems to have plenty of demand for now, with issuers able to offer relatively cheap borrowing rates. Meta's Beignet Investor issuance carried a coupon of 6.6%, or just a percentage point above Meta's outstanding corporate bonds. The debt issued by TeraWulf and Cipher Mining carried coupons that weren't much higher than the Beignet debt. De Boltz said the returns have been attractive for bond investors, who have been bidding up the value of the debt after it's issued. Data center debt has returned some 10% and 11% so far this year, which translates to a 20% annual return, he said. If returns fall closer to 4% to 5%, investors may step back, he said, but aside from a few isolated incidents there hasn't been much evidence of that. Investors like "the risk and more and more people are buying the product," he said. While the market is working well for issuers, it does carry risks for investors due to the limited disclosure the borrowers provide. There's also the fact that the bonds are often bought by mutual funds even though retail investors can't buy them directly, which could draw broader scrutiny if data center developments sour. The Pimco Income Fund, for example, held $4.2 billion of the Beignet Investor bonds at the end of March, accounting for 1.88% of the portfolio, according to public Pimco disclosures. Roughly a third of the fund's assets are in share classes marketed to retail investors. The Bridge Builder Core Plus Bond Fund, which is only available to clients of the Edward Jones retail brokerage, held $268 million at the end of March, or 0.58% of the portfolio. That creep into retail points to a broader issue with using the 144A market as a work-around. AI companies have found an insatiable need to source funding wherever it may lead them, and lines are blurring as public markets go private while tech startups piggyback off public companies' access to capital. The question now is whether the broader market appetite for AI financing will finally hit its limit.

item.title: OpenAI Researcher Says GPT-5.6 is Better at AI Research Than Most Human Interns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: I'm reporting from Seoul, where thousands of AI researchers from around the world have gathered for this year's International Conference on Machine Learning. One of the most popular spots at the conference is OpenAI's booth, which has been consistently encircled by a line of young AI PhDs. They're waiting for the chance to talk to OpenAI researchers and recruiters or try their hand at an arcade-style claw machine whose prizes include Codex-themed Rubrik's Cubes and fidget spinners. OpenAI had potentially bad news for those PhDs, however-human internships are likely to be in short supply at the company. Senior OpenAI researcher Noam Brown told me he would choose the company's latest announced model, GPT-5.6, over a human research intern for most tasks! He was responding to my question about whether the company is making progress toward an automated, AI-powered research intern. CEO Sam Altman said in October last year he believed the company would have such an AI by September this year.
